rules.classification: Spectroscopic classes and alert or messenger labels are different definitions and are not compared; two active classes differ when neither label refines the other (for example 'SN Ia' and 'SN Ia-91T' agree); an earlier value from the same provider is a revision.
rules.host: Two proposed hosts agree when their names match after case and spacing are ignored or one name is among the other's NED cross-identifications; otherwise they are an identity ambiguity. Association probabilities are not computed.
rules.photometry: Only exactly compatible photometry (same epoch, band, system, method, calibration and direct/difference state, two or more providers) is compared. The limiting magnitude or flux that a provider reports alongside a detection is that epoch's detection threshold, not a non-detection, and is not compared with the detection; a detection brighter than another provider's non-detection limit at the same epoch is a status conflict. A group is listed only when it is still inconsistent under these rules; at most 10 groups per event, most significant first.
rules.position: Two positions with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they are more than 2 arcsec apart; when one states an error radius, the separation is compared with 3 times that radius.
rules.redshift: Two redshifts with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 0.005 (about 1,500 km/s); transient and host redshifts are different definitions and are listed, not compared; host redshifts of differently named hosts are an identity ambiguity.
rules.revision: A retracted row, or a superseded row of the same provider whose value differs beyond the property's rule, is a revision or retraction; a revision within the rule is consistent; the earlier value stays visible.
rules.sigma: Two values that both state an uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 3 combined standard deviations (uncertainties added in quadrature; a stated position error radius is treated as one standard deviation).

evidence_timeline.summary: Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) are well-known standardisable candles, and are one of the main ways to measure the distance to their host galaxies. However, extinction due to interstellar dust causes objects to appear fainter and redder. Correcting for this requires estimating the amount of intervening material and how the extinction changes as a function of wavelength. We present and analyse optical and near-infrared data of the well-observed SN 2024gy and use these to compare different extinction estimation techniques, making use of photometric, spectroscopic, and polarimetric data. SN 2024gy is a normal SN Ia with high velocity (HV) components in Si IIλ6355 (phase < -10 days) and a particularly strong HV feature in the Ca II near-infrared triplet (up to peak). Modelling SN 2024gy with TARDIS shows better matches with a double-detonation scenario compared to a delayed-detonation scenario due to a better match to the Ca II HV component. A measurement of the stable Ni/Fe ratio, however, favours a delayed-detonation scenario. Host extinction estimates range from E(B - V)<SUB>host</SUB> = 0.12 ± 0.02 mag (narrow interstellar absorption lines) to E(B - V)<SUB>host</SUB> = 0.24 ± 0.06 mag (Lira law) with a mean of E(B - V)<SUB>host</SUB> = 0.22 ± 0.04 mag, assuming R<SUB>V</SUB> = 3.1. The spread between different methods highlights the challenge of accurately estimating the amount of extinction light suffers before being observed.
evidence_timeline.title: An analysis of the Type Ia SN 2024gy and a comparison of different host extinction estimation techniques

evidence_timeline.summary: Time-domain astrophysics continues to grow rapidly, with the inception of new surveys drastically increasing data volumes. Democratized, distributed approaches to training sets for machine learning classifiers are crucial to make the most of this torrent of discovery - with citizen science approaches proving effective at meeting these requirements. In this paper, we describe the creation of and the initial results from the Kilonova Seekers citizen science project, built to find transient phenomena from the GOTO telescopes in near real-time. Kilonova Seekers launched in 2023 July and received over 600 000 classifications from approximately 2000 volunteers over the course of the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA O4a observing run. During this time, the project has yielded 20 discoveries, generated a 'gold-standard' training set of 17 682 detections for augmenting deep-learned classifiers, and measured the performance and biases of Zooniverse volunteers on real-bogus classification. This project will continue throughout the lifetime of GOTO, pushing candidates at ever-greater cadence, and directly facilitate the next-generation classification algorithms currently in development.
evidence_timeline.title: Kilonova Seekers: the GOTO project for real-time citizen science in time-domain astrophysics

evidence_timeline.summary:
Supernovae are important for various reasons, from stellar explosive mechanisms, synthesis of heavy elements and enrichment of the interstellar medium, to cosmological distance determination. They are studied with a variety of observational tools and techniques: different telescopes from gamma and X-ray to radio, neutrino underground detectors, spectroscopy, and computational simulations. Additionally, surveys and monitoring programs are used to detect and track supernovae, providing valuable data for understanding their diversity and evolution. There are dedicated websites (e.g. Latest SNe) and SN-detection and photometry software (e.g. the Sehgal Observatory Supernova Search Tool, Starblinker, CCDSoft, Astrometrica, MPO Canopus, SExtractor, others).

The Al-Khatm Observatory (exact location), despite having a relatively small telescope, has good features (an excellent mount, near-IR filters, remotely controlled and fully programmable) and 300+ clear skies per year with low observational subscriptions; with stacking, it can reach magnitudes of 21 in the Ic band. We conduct a program of supernova observations and photometric analysis, fitting a number of bright SNe (SN2023wrk, SN2024bch, SN2024gy, SN2024any, others) with templates to determine their types and progenitor characteristics and comparing with data obtained by other observatories and analysts.
evidence_timeline.title: Recent supernovae observations and type/model fitting

However, extinction due to interstellar dust causes objects to appear fainter and redder. Correcting for this requires estimating the amount of intervening material and how the extinction changes as a function of wavelength. We present and analyse optical and near-infrared data of the well-observed SN 2024gy and use these to compare different extinction estimation techniques, making use of photometric, spectroscopic, and polarimetric data. Democratized, distributed approaches to training sets for machine learning classifiers are crucial to make the most of this torrent of discovery - with citizen science approaches proving effective at meeting these requirements. publication_revisions.abstract:
Supernovae are important for various reasons, from stellar explosive mechanisms, synthesis of heavy elements and enrichment of the interstellar medium, to cosmological distance determination. They are studied with a variety of observational tools and techniques: different telescopes from gamma and X-ray to radio, neutrino underground detectors, spectroscopy, and computational simulations. Additionally, surveys and monitoring programs are used to detect and track supernovae, providing valuable data for understanding their diversity and evolution. There are dedicated websites (e.g. Latest SNe) and SN-detection and photometry software (e.g. the Sehgal Observatory Supernova Search Tool, Starblinker, CCDSoft, Astrometrica, MPO Canopus, SExtractor, others).

The Al-Khatm Observatory (exact location), despite having a relatively small telescope, has good features (an excellent mount, near-IR filters, remotely controlled and fully programmable) and 300+ clear skies per year with low observational subscriptions; with stacking, it can reach magnitudes of 21 in the Ic band. We conduct a program of supernova observations and photometric analysis, fitting a number of bright SNe (SN2023wrk, SN2024bch, SN2024gy, SN2024any, others) with templates to determine their types and progenitor characteristics and comparing with data obtained by other observatories and analysts.

Each retained row passed a mission-specific past-release check; XMM also required data_in_heasarc=Y and NICER required VALIDATED. No file bytes were downloaded.

The adapter is anonymous and restricted to the provider-documented public AllWISE Source Catalog and 2MASS Point Source Catalog. It stores catalog rows and official links only; proprietary/exclusive-access IRSA holdings are outside the allowlist.

The anonymous public NED TAP service documents programmatic cone searches of the NED Object Directory and requests NED acknowledgment. CTAS retains bounded source-native rows and provenance only. NOIRLab's provider-owned API authentication notebook states that anyone may retrieve public files while proprietary-file retrieval requires authorization. This adapter sends no credential and retains a product only after an exact file-metadata lookup supplies a nonblank release_date no later than the query time. Anonymous metadata about unreleased files is counted only for exclusion and is never stored. Product bytes are not downloaded.

Rubin alert packets are world-public with no proprietary period, and Fink documents its LSST Science Portal and REST API as real-time, public services requiring no login. Coordinate and first-detection proximity are not proof of source identity.

SIMBAD documents free access without registration under the ODbL license. This adapter uses the anonymous official TAP service for one bounded coordinate query, retains provider attribution and source bibcodes, and does not treat a nearby literature object as the transient, its host, or a new detection.

rules.classification: Spectroscopic classes and alert or messenger labels are different definitions and are not compared; two active classes differ when neither label refines the other (for example 'SN Ia' and 'SN Ia-91T' agree); an earlier value from the same provider is a revision.
rules.host: Two proposed hosts agree when their names match after case and spacing are ignored or one name is among the other's NED cross-identifications; otherwise they are an identity ambiguity. Association probabilities are not computed.
rules.photometry: Only exactly compatible photometry (same epoch, band, system, method, calibration and direct/difference state, two or more providers) is compared. The limiting magnitude or flux that a provider reports alongside a detection is that epoch's detection threshold, not a non-detection, and is not compared with the detection; a detection brighter than another provider's non-detection limit at the same epoch is a status conflict. A group is listed only when it is still inconsistent under these rules; at most 10 groups per event, most significant first.
rules.position: Two positions with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they are more than 2 arcsec apart; when one states an error radius, the separation is compared with 3 times that radius.
rules.redshift: Two redshifts with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 0.005 (about 1,500 km/s); transient and host redshifts are different definitions and are listed, not compared; host redshifts of differently named hosts are an identity ambiguity.
rules.revision: A retracted row, or a superseded row of the same provider whose value differs beyond the property's rule, is a revision or retraction; a revision within the rule is consistent; the earlier value stays visible.
rules.sigma: Two values that both state an uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 3 combined standard deviations (uncertainties added in quadrature; a stated position error radius is treated as one standard deviation).
